utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, Alex Demirdjian, with Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any matters which arise before we call the -- we have the witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Surprisingly not, Your Honours, but just wanting to sure that everybody in the courtroom received the notice we sent last night about the additional adjudicated fact that the witness may cover. This was supposed to be covered by Witness ST-252, but since he has been withdrawn, this witness can address the issue of destroyed churches and mosques. So I just wanted to make sure if there was any objection to that or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you were about to rise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We object to the adjudicated fact 1219 being testified by the next witness. The next witness, 008, was in contact with the Prosecution back in 1999. Then, again in 2000, and then in 2003, and probably last year when they included him in their 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt Mr. Aleksic briefly to go back to Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You said that this witness could testify, et cetera. And you referred to the witness who was withdrawn. The way it is phrased is as an observation. Is there a clear application from the Prosecution to which Mr. Aleksic has already began -- to enter his objection, but could I hear precisely what your application is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This witness is called to deal with adjudicated facts 504, 509, 934 and 936. What the Prosecution is asking at this moment is for the witness to be able to testify also in relation to adjudicated fact 1219, which also deals with partially -- some of the adjudicated facts he is already supposed to cover are kind of included in adjudicated fact 1219 as it deals with Serb paramilitaries being and killing people in the town of Teslic. That's already covered by the first four adjudicated facts I mentioned. It's the second part of that adjudicated fact which says that, "destroyed and damaged Muslim and Croat property, including mosques and Catholic churches." So that would be our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you had said something about 252 having been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Wouldn't the implication of that being that the Prosecution had abandoned the intention of -- of leading the fact to which he was going to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, if you remember this was the witness that we were intending to subpoena and in the end we withdrew our application. This is another crime base witness from the municipality of Teslic. And as we were about to -- we did submit a subpoena but we withdrew that application. However, we are still relying on the evidence. Most of the evidence that 252 could have covered have been covered by the first witness who testified about Teslic a few months ago. And the rest are also covered by the current witness. We're just left with this one adjudicated fact, which is 1219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, continue, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Since 1992, the -- witness was in contact with the Prosecution for a number of years and he never mentioned at all the adjudicated fact that the Prosecution would like him to testify to. This witness was scheduled to testify in late November or early December last year, which was a good opportunity for them to notify us through a proofing note or in any other way that he wished to testify that. Then we were informed that this witness is unable to appear in person and that a videolink was to be established on the 24th of January. So there was another contact that they had with him but nothing happened. Now, with relation to this adjudicated fact, Witness 252 should have testified. In their motion submitted on the 28th of October, they informed both the Chamber and the Defence that ST-252 would be testifying in the week beginning the 1st of November, and according to their notice it was scheduled for this witness 252 to appear on Friday, the 5th of November. Only one day before, on the 4th of November, Ms. Pidwell on transcript page 16927, said that they would withdraw their motion asking for the subpoena and that they would also withdraw the -- ST-252 witness from their list. Therefore, it seems to me that it was a decision made by the OTP to give up on the evidence to be given by this particular witness and his covering this adjudicated facts. However, if the Chamber allows the next witness, ST-008, to give evidence on this adjudicated fact as well, I have to tell you that I haven't prepared myself for any questions in that relation. I may not have any questions, though, but I will let you know in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we join the Zupljanin Defence's position on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anything in reply, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honours. Mr. Aleksic was mentioning at the end of page 3 that the witness never mentioned at all the adjudicated fact. In fact there is an information note which was provided to the Defence with the ERN 00768078, and at the last page there's a mention: "All the mosques in Teslic were destroyed, as were Catholic churches, and the witness heard," et cetera, et cetera. So that's for the first point. The second point is that clearly that Mr. Aleksic is not caught by surprise. It appears that he had already prepared for ST-252 to address this issue and as he said that witness was supposed to testify on the 5th of November and only withdrawn the day before. So, clearly, this is not a new topic. This is something that he had prepared for cross-examining ST-252, obviously. He just hasn't prepared in terms of this witness. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber having considered counsel's application and response is of the view that the application should be denied, for the reason that the evidence is -- appears to be repetitive, and in any event deviates from the principles to which we have adhered in terms of these witnesses called to deal with denied adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honours. One last reminder that the witness has protective measures of pseudonym, face and voice distortion, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, one information. We have been able to finally identify the book where the 1D MFI documents which I tried to introduce into the evidence during the -- the -- the cross-examination of expert Brown, we located which book it is. It the book of -- written by Mr. Slavko Lisica, actually the author of these documents. It is called, "The Commander Without a Need." It was published in 2000. On page 5 of the -- of the preface, the Colonel Lisica acknowledges that the documents are his own -- the documents which are put in the book. We copied the book and we sent the copy to our learned friends to review that, and I just talked to Mr. Hannis before the -- before the beginning, and he said that he would need another day or so to review that and give us back his opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Which document is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's -- I believe, Your Honours, it is 1D263 MFI and 1D264 MFI. But there is -- as you remember, there's -- there 's another set of maybe seven or eight documents which are -- which have the same -- the same problem actually. We wanted them introduced into the evidence and the Office of the Prosecutor opposed that. So hopefully we will resolve the matter and inform the Trial Chamber accordingly. I just wanted to inform you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, you had something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to indicate that the Prosecution indeed does have a continued objection to this. I need a little further time to address it because Ms. Korner was present when it first came up and is more familiar with it. But it's my understanding at the time, I think on the 19th of January when this was discussed, Ms. Korner raised the issue that this document appeared to be from a book because it had the number 137 at the bottom of the documents, and at that time Mr. Zecevic said, "I don't have any indication nor I can say that this is a book. This might be, as far as I'm concerned, might be the archive." Now it appears that it's clearly a book, and our position is, in essence, this is not much different than a media report or else it's an attempt to get around Rule 92 and put in the written evidence of a witness who's not present in court and the requirements of Rule 92 haven't been complied with. So I have further submissions to make and I would like an opportunity to be able to do that either later today or tomorrow, after I've had a further chance to research it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will have to return to this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may be seated, if that's more comfortable for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I -- I take it from your answers that can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming for -- to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now, then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The usher will now show you a piece of paper with your data, your date of birth, your name and surname, and so on. Please verify the data are correct, and, if so, we would like to you sign the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, I think there's a mistake on -- on that paper. Can I see it again, please? The surname was misspelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll get another one printed and brought down and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Witness. There will be another of these sheets for you to sign but there was an error in this one. My next question, Mr. Witness, and I should add, that we refer to you not with your name but with either saying Mr. Witness or saying Witness ST-008, that is your pseudonym, and that's not a sign of disrespect but that is because of -- we want to avoid to give your name to the public. We decided to do so. Is this the first time you testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then explain to you briefly how the proceedings will unfold here. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, who is sitting to your right, and the Prosecution has asked for, altogether, two hours to examine you in-chief. After that, the counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting to your left, has asked for two-hours to cross-examine you. And when Mr. Zecevic is through with his cross-examination, Mr. Krgovic, who is directly behind Mr. Zecevic, will cross-examine you as well, and he asked for one hour. And when Mr. Krgovic is through, we will give the floor back to the Prosecution who will have a chance to put some final questions to you in light of the answers you have been given during cross-examination. And during all that, and even after that, the Judges may have questions for you as well. Now, as a practical matter, the recordings here are taken on videotape on and tape and these tapes have to be changed every 90 minutes, which means that every hour and a half, we will have a break of 20 minutes. But if, for any reason you need an additional break or you have some kind of trouble, please, tell us and we will try to accommodate you. That's all I have to say for the moment. Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like to start with some questions about your background. Can you indicate to the Court what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And in which town were you born?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: In Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is correct to say that you lived your entire life in Teslic, until you had to leave in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that you went through your military service in 1975 and 1976?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what was your profession prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I was a property developer, until 1988. In 1988, I had an accident and fell off my house, so I had to go to hospital in Zagreb and then after that, to Varazdinske Toplice spa and all together I spent about a year in a wheelchair, and after that, I had to use crutches that can you see me walking with today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: As a result of this accident, was there an assessment as to your medical condition?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes. I was declared 80 per cent disabled, but up to this date, I did not receive any final decision. That was a provisional decision, and it -- it defined me as an 80-per cent invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Following this accident, is it correct to say that you had a grocery store in Teslic and this is where you remained?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I stayed there, because the shop was registered in my wife's name, and it was on the ground floor of my house. It was a convenience store, and everybody from the former Yugoslavia knows exactly what that means. I don't know how you call it around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I'd like to take you to the year 1992, and I'd like to take you to the time where you were arrested. Just a few days before your arrest, did you notice any activity in your town?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Not only a few days before. You could notice even it months before that. Officially, however, on 2nd of June, in the morning, I was awoken by loud noises on the street, and when I looked in that direction I saw tanks. Then I woke up my wife. I told her, Get up. This is something very unusual. Then we went up to the terrace and watched the tanks move up to the barracks. Close to my house, there used to be some sort of a barracks for the reserve army forces. And then there was also another barracks, JNA barracks, down the street. So my wife and I were watching them from our terrace and those tanks and trucks went up to that barracks. We couldn't understand why that was happening, where they are going, or anything like that. Up to that point, I used to watch all that. It seemed normal to me. There was a war in Croatia, so you would expect that to happen. But, then, at the moment, nothing was clear to me. Why would those tanks come to our barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, is it correct to say that the very next day, on the 3rd of June, 1992, you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Immediately, the following day. I was sitting in front of my store. There was an uncle and a neighbour of mine there as well, and even one Serb from Gornji Teslic. The place is called Zorani. So we were all sitting in front of the store and drinking rakija. And we all talked about things in general and then suddenly we saw two cars moving towards the house. The first was a red Golf. There were no registration plates on it. Behind it, there was also a Golf in regular police colours, so they came in front of the house. There's about 20 or 30 metres between the road and the house itself. We continued sitting down, and then they got out from the red Golf. There were three of them. They were wearing uniforms and red berets. And from the blue police car, four men got out. As soon as they were out of the car, they cocked their weapon -- they are weapons and stood by the car. (redacted) (redacted) And they told me, You have to come with us. Where? To the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we redact that last part, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to be careful not to mention your name, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No problem. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: So I said, Can I get my crutches? Because if you are taking me to the station I won't be able to get into the station over the stairs if I don't have the crutches or somebody would have to help me. I know how it looks like. They told me, No. You can't take your crutches because you're not going to need them. So I got into the car, as instructed. It was the red car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us a moment ago that four men got out of the police car. Can you tell the Court if you recognised any of these men?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I recognised two of them. They used to be active policemen during the former Yugoslavia. I recognised Mirko Bubic. The other two were the reserve policemen in the former Yugoslavia. So I used to know those two people because they were policemen for quite a long period. So I got into the car on the back seat. Then they drove backwards, the police car, and the red car made a U-turn in front of my car -- in front of my house. They went back to the road that goes to Banja Luka and started driving towards Teslic. We went to a place called Baric. You could see tank obstacles there. That same day, in the morning, I was in town, because I had to fetch milk and bread for my store. There were no obstacles then. And then when they took me there, there were already obstacles at the cross-roads that leads to Barici. While they were driving, they opened the car window, they played Chetnik songs, people at the check-points simply raised their hands with three fingers and we were allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Just a couple of matters I'd like to go back to. You said that you were put into the red car. These are the man in camouflage and the red berets. Did you know any of the men in that car?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no. Nobody in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the policemen; you mentioned the name of Mirko Bubic. And you said four men in total in the police car. What were they wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: They wore normal blue police uniforms, the way they used to look before the war. That was the regular police. The reserve police used to wear blue camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And besides Mirko Bubic, did you recognise the other three men? Did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: The ones in the red car? No. No, I didn't know them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the ones in the police car?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I told you, I recognised Mirko Bubic, Aleksa Petrovic, and the guy, I think his name is Celar. I know that his nickname is Celar. I don't know his name. I also know where he used to live. But I wouldn't know his name, his nickname is Celar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. When I interrupted you, you were talking about them playing Chetnik songs and driving along. Where did they take you to?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: They took me to the police station. When they turned towards the police station, I knew that place. I was born there. This is a roundabout right in front of the police station, and there is also a park there and a big pine tree right in the middle of the roundabout. You could see lots of policemen there, various kinds camouflage uniforms. You couldn't really know who those people were. And I simply observed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just before we get into the next phase. When you were arrested and put into that car, were you given any reasons for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: No, no. They didn't tell me anything. When they took me, I told team that I needed my crutches, and they simply told me, You are not going to need them. What their plans were, that, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what happened when you reached the police station?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: That red Golf in which I was was then stopped in front of the station and then they pushed me out and I told them, I can't get out so simply. It was a two-door car so it wasn't easy to get out. I needed help for that. I had to take out my legs one by one and one of them told me, Faster, and I told him, No, I can't go faster. I don't have my crutches. He told me, Get in there. And I told him, I cannot go inside without my crutches. You can kill you if you want but I can't. He started swearing my mother and I told him, You can just kill me right here because I cannot go up the stairs unless I crawl. I cannot walk up the stairs. Then one of them, I don't know which one, pulled me by the hair and pushed me, and I told him again, You can kill me if you want, that's all. Then I could hear that somebody slapped him on the hand. That's what I heard. And then he released me. And he ordered me to get in. I came to the stairs and then I couldn't get in. On top of the stairs there was another policeman. He also told me, Get in. And I said, I can't unless you help me. And then that man helped me. I got inside. When I was getting inside, to the right side was the new duty room and to the left was some sort of waiting-room and in the middle there was a staircase leading up to the upper floor. I don't remember quite whether there was one or two upper floors. So, this policeman told me to go to the waiting-room, on the left. And when I went there, I saw a man standing by the wall with his hands in the air. He was showing three fingers, like this, his legs were spread, and he was standing by the wall. That policeman ordered him to do that. I told them, Well, I cannot possibly go through things like that. You can kill me if you want, but I can't. And then he went out towards the duty room, and the guy by the wall turned and I say that that was the man who used to be a trading standards officer in the Teslic municipality. I asked him, Why did you come here? I don't know. He asked me, Why did you come here? I don't know. Can you help me? They ordered me to empty pockets and I told them that I couldn't possibly do that, because I cannot bend. If I sit, maybe then I could do it. Then I asked Asir to help me and then we took off my shoelaces, we took out my keys, car keys and my house keys and gave all that to the policeman, which he took to the duty room. After that, he came back and told us to go, so we followed him. We went out, Asir helped me to get down the stairs. He took us to another building. That's where the jail was, in the basement. Again, there was stairs, I don't know how many stairs. That was the first time that I entered the jail. I didn't know that before. The stairs were quite wide so two or three people abreast could go down the stairs. So when the two of us, Asir and I got in, the policeman unlocked the doors, and we saw four or five people inside. Now, I recognised Fadil Rasulovic, deputy bank manager, then his brother, they used to call him Fiko [as interpreted] but I don't quite remember his name. I know that he used to be his brother and they used to call him Fiko. I thought that I had to be very close to the microphone but, all right, thank you. So there was an elderly man, probably older than 70. His name was Mandzukic. They used to have patisseries, burek shops and things like that. So his name was Mandzukic. Then there was another guy called Gilic, and Anto Tabak. He was a photographer and he was a well known person there. And then there was also me and Asir. So there were people coming in and out, people taken in, taken out. They used to hit us. They used to hit those who were taken out. You could hear some screams. I hope that I won't go through something like that in my life again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned to us that you saw the people you just named, about four or five people. Did that number vary eventually?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Every day, every hour, every 10 or 15 minutes they would come and bring some people and take some other people out. There were four to 50 of us in that room. At some point we couldn't sit. We had to stand up. People used to sit each in the -- used to stand up even in the toilet. You could smell the ammonia from the urine. So it was quite unbearable. The tears used to come out of our eyes because of the smell of the ammonia. We used to shout, Give us some air or kill us, because we needed some air. So I think on the 12th day, we heard some sort of noise and then a policeman came in and he told us, You should go out in a column up with by one. So we got out --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, just before we get to that point, I have a few questions about the prison building. You first told us there was another building. Where was this located in relation to the police station?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, how should I tell you? It's close to the main road but it's separate from the building of the police station. There's maybe five, six, or ten metres between them. I can't be very precise about it. So there's maybe 10 metres between that building and the police station building, or maybe even less. It's an L-shaped complex. Also the Teslic Radio used to be there. Political parties used to have their offices there. I don't quite remember everything. And in the basement was the jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the transcripts don't record the numbers correctly. You gave the number of people that were held with you in total. Can you repeat that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, the number would vary. From four to 50, 40 to 50 maybe. There were 40 to 50 of us when they put us into the bus. How big was that room four by four or three by four, I wouldn't know. We had to stand up. I myself I lied down because I couldn't bear to stand up all the time and then other people used to trample on me. There was simply not enough room, not enough room to sit and let alone to lay down. The floor was made from the concrete and there were many of us. But, still, there was simply not enough space.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned to us that on the 12th day you were ordered to be put on the bus. Before that, during those 12 days, were you provided any food?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Let me tell you; I don't remember exactly which day it was. I think it was the fourth or the fifth day. It was Bajram. And that day we received one sandwich each. It was the fourth, the fifth day; I'm not sure. It was the first day of Bajram. That's when we received the sandwich each. Sometimes they would give us a canister of water and it was simply one drop of water per each person because there were 50 of us, 40 or 50 to us and you had to divide ten litres of water to 50 people. Everyone would scream, Give me water, Give me water. We were hungry but we still needed water to freshen up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that as people were being brought in and out of the cell they were hit. How often did the hitting occur?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Not only when people were taken out, also when people were brought in. When there were just a few of us they would get in, one, two, or three of them, and to tell you the truth as soon as they appeared in the door, we would have to stand up and start singing songs. Izet Mandzukic and I - he used to be a teacher - and also Fadil's brother, Frke, they knew the songs. I never heard of those songs, so they were quite helpful, because then we were not beaten as much. If you didn't know the song, it was a different story. He would appear at the door, he would tell you, Go, sing, and I've never heard the song before. So Frke and Izet Mandzukic knew the songs. I don't know how come they knew the songs so they would start and we would follow them singing. And then we would receive less beatings if we were singing. But we had to turn our backs to them so it could be your own brother behind and you wouldn't be able to know. However you would be able to sometimes recognise voices. So in a space of a few days, I was able to recognise voices of the people who would come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you told us that this would mean when you were singing that you would receive less beatings. Does that mean that you personally were beaten too inside the police station?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: In the police station I only received one blow with a baton. I mean, I don't know how that happened. But when we were in the Territorial Defence, we were beaten more and later on even more. To be fair, I was only hit once with a baton on my back. I always used to stand by the wall. I knew exactly what my health was and I knew that I wouldn't be able to go through that. So whoever was closest to the door would get hit the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you recognise any of the men who were bringing in detainees?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, it could be your own brother but they were behind you, and you had to stand facing the wall. So you could only recognise voices, if you knew some people. I only recognised one of them by his voice because he used to be my neighbour on Zuc. I have no idea how I ended up in the reserve police. He was a ruin of a man, a failure. I don't know whether he managed to finish any schools or whether he managed to finish any apprenticeship. He was a problem child. He used to steal from his mother and his father. And then he would spend that money on us, who didn't have any money. So when he appeared in the police I really didn't know how that happened. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Page 21, line 15, Your Honours, can we redact the witness's first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to take you back to the point where you told us that after 12 days you were put on a bus. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I guess we should also redact the name of the neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. The nickname, yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber where you were taken when you were put on the bus.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know where they were taking us. We wondered about it. We were driven in the bus for some 15 to 20 minutes, and the bus stopped in front of the hangar of the Territorial Defence. That's where the Territorial Defence used to be before the war. When we were in the bus we had to keep our heads down below. Nobody was allowed to raise their heads above the seats. I myself, of course, couldn't resist so I was trying to look to see where they were taking us and when I saw that we were going towards Gomjenica, I thought that they were going towards the Vlajic and the mines; I didn't know they were taking us to the TO building. And when we took turn towards the hangar, that's when I saw where we were. Then they ordered us to go out from the bus and to line up. So we lined up in the front of the hangar. We went out one by one. I saw various vehicles, military, civilian. It's as if there was some sort of a meeting and so many cars arrived there. So that's where we lined up and then they ordered us to enter the hangar. And then we went through some sort of a corridor and then we entered the hall. Inside the corridor there was police. On both sides, left and right, there were members of the police. There was a table where their guns were and they held batons in their hands. So some of us were hit; some of us were not. And then we entered this huge hangar. I have never been there before. I knew that was a TO building but I had no idea that it was so big. In the police station, we didn't have enough space; in hangar, it was a different situation. It was a huge place and it was very cold. In the police station, it was very hot and there was a stench of ammonia; and in the hangar it was huge and cold. So that's how it was. We remained there and then all the time, various vehicles and vans would bring more people, four, five, ten people would be brought to the hangar. So, in the end, there was about 200 or 250 of us. Now, at that point, we weren't that cold anymore because of respiration. However, we did have to sleep on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that when you arrived there was a lineup of policemen inside in the corridor. Did you recognise any of the policemen inside the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: At that point in time, I didn't recognise any of them. As far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court -- you just told us there were about 200 or 250 people held in the TO warehouse. Did you notice or did you know what was the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: We all knew that the people in there were all Muslims and Croats. There wasn't a single Serb there with us. There was no reason for them to be there, as they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that when you arrived there was this corridor and policemen with batons, some were hit, some were not. Were there other occurrences of beatings throughout your detention in the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: There were such situations. When we were inside, three, four, or five of them would come in at a time and start hitting people randomly. When they got tired, then they would start shouting, All of you, Balijas and Ustashas should be killed, and then they would leave. Then they would leave us in peace for an hour or two, or, at times, even a day or two. It all depended on their mood and what the plan was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court if you recognised any of the men who were beating the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Having in mind my health, I wasn't in a very good position to be able to abide by their rules. On one occasion I simply fell to the ground because my legs cut off and I was lying on the concrete. I was able to see them then but I was told to cover my head with my hands. In any case, I managed to peep sometimes; on other occasions I didn't dare. It depended on how I felt. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: How could I know? They could put on whatever they wanted. They seemed to have some ranks, but I don't know what the titles or the ranks were. It was their internal arrangement between Marinko, Tomo, and Predrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he had any role in the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: He probably did, because he beat us the most. After I left, though, I don't know whether he resumed that practice or whether it was taken up by someone else. But as far as I could see, he beat the people there the most. They all did, but he seemed to be the most bloodthirsty of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber individual instances of beating that you witnessed, that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: They all came in and left. I don't know why this Gilic person stood out. He used to be a high school teacher in Teslic. They all seemed to be looking for him, but Tomo expressly asked for Sandzaklija. In any case, they beat him the most by that point in time I wasn't able to stand, but they seemed to have taken him out of the line, put him against a wall, and beat him there. Tomo beat him the most. He had a wooden stick and a chain which he used to hit him. I don't know how he managed to find such an item. Whenever a person would be hit with that chain over the head, it would sound as -- a concrete, a piece of concrete was struck. They beat everyone, but he seemed to beat Gilic the most. Then he was taken outside. Whether it was that he died at that point in time or later on, I don't know. But I just saw him being taken out. I don't know whether he died on the spot or not. In any case I never saw him or heard of him again. There was a Croat too who worked in the electrical utility company. When they hooked my house into the network he was there, and that's how I knew him. They tried to patch me in. He used to be a private entrepreneur, and he did some work for the utility company. He was their contractor. There was another person from Barici with him whose last name I can't recall but he was another Croat. The two of them came to do the electrical wiring in the house, and I saw them in the warehouse again. Tomo also singled him out, calling him Ustasha, asking him what he was doing there, threatening to show him what he deserved. Tomo beat that Croat a lot. After a beating, he would leave for quarter of an hour, then come back, and he would say -- he said, Is Tudjman dead? Referring to the Croat. He was about 10 metres away from me, so I couldn't see whether he was dead or not. In any case, he was taken out the way Gilic was. I don't know whether he succumbed to the wounds at that point in time or later on; I wasn't close enough to see. But, in any case, no one heard of him later on or saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was there any other instances of beatings that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: There were. If I had the time to sit down and write it all, I would remember things much more clearly, and if I had been able to do that at the time, it would have been better. But it is very different to put all the pieces of the puzzle in their right place. A lot of things happened. I think Himzo Jasarevic was with us and his brother was some kind of commander in the former Yugoslavia. I don't know whether he was a captain or something of the sort. In any case, he was a military officer. He was in Tesanj, in the Bosnian army at the time. Brane Milicic had a group we called Sarenjaci and whenever they came in, the worse things happened. Four of five of them would pick on a single person and it was dreadful. I used to know Brane because I used to sell some stuff in the black market and Brano used to buy things from me and he would re-sell it at a higher price later. So we had known each other from before, from the early 1990s. I recognised his voice when he shouted, but he didn't care. He didn't care we were acquaintances. He didn't strike me, though, because I was down on the concrete. The rest of the group asked me, Why are you on the floor, Balija? And then they would kick me, if they felt like it. In any case, Brane beat up Himzo in the meantime. They used to be neighbours in Barici towards Ruzevici or Ruzevacke Bare whatever the place is. They had known each other. He beat Himzo heavily. He shouted and hit him, saying, You're here, and your brother is killing Serbs right now. I'm going to send a couple of shells down there. And I have you, while they're attacking us. Himzo was covered in blood. He even peed blood. He was able to withstand that for a day or two, but Brane kept coming back and he finished him off. He was then taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before we carry on with this after the break, I received a copy of the pseudonym sheet, if we can have the witness sign it again with the correct spelling of his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, could I put a question to you. These chaps that you have mentioned, Tomo and Brane, and others, were you able to distinguish by their uniforms or by your knowledge, whether they belonged to the police or to the army or whether they were paramilitaries? Do you know under whose authority they were acting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you are familiar with the uniforms by now. In any case, the people hailing from that area know uniforms, especially those who had served their military service or whoever came into contact with the police, and people could tell apart regular policemen from reserve policemen. We knew which uniforms were worn by soldiers and which by the reserve force of the military or the military police. Brane Milicic had a camouflage military uniform, similar to an American camouflage combat fatigue. It was similar. The other one had camouflage blue uniform of the reserve force and also an olive-drab reserve uniform. That's as far as uniforms go. It's very simple to tell them apart if you are from that part of the world. No further explanation is needed usually as to who wore what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may proceed with the signature of the sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's now admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1801, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] and we take the break now and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I carry on, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go back to the last topic that the Judge was asking you about. You mentioned the uniform of Mr. Milicic and the transcript is not perfectly clear as to what Mr. Tomo Mihajlovic was wearing. Could you clarify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Tomo Mihajlovic wore a blue uniform of the reserve police force, a camouflage blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And earlier today you told us that -- you mentioned Mr. Mihajlovic in the context of Mr. Predrag Markocevic and Marinko Djukic. Can you tell us anything about the relationship of Tomo Mihajlovic with these two men?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Predrag Markocevic, before the elections, used to be an inspector. I don't know what kind of inspector though, I think a crime inspector. Marinko Djukic was a policeman, who had a fire-fighting certificate so he worked as a fire-fighting inspector. Tomo worked in Teslic in a raw material warehouse or dump. That's where he worked. I don't know how the three of them banded together; perhaps by party line. In any case, they were doing their utmost to prove themselves, and that's why I believed -- believe they grouped together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You just told us that you don't know how they banded together. What is it that you saw that leaded [sic] you to the conclusion that they banded together?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, we could see it. I could see them moving about town. They were uniforms, especially in the evening when we went out. They wore the Chetnik hats with the -- with kokades. That's how they stood out and you could see them together. You could see them in the afternoon, after office hours walking about town together. I wasn't only the only one who saw them; many people in Teslic saw them walking around in uniform and with the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us earlier about Brane Milicic coming into the TO warehouse with a man called Sarenjaci. Could you tell us who else was accompanying him, when coming to the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I didn't know those guys. There were four or five of them who came as part of that group. They had camouflage uniforms of the reserve military force, not the police. They were our nightmare, so to say. After we learned that -- after that, we learned that Brane and his group destroyed all of the mosques there were. We heard it from others. I didn't see that myself, and I didn't see them destroying them. I only heard rumours from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you know the names or the nicknames of the men who accompanied Brane when they came to the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: No, just Brane. I only knew him, because we were in the market-place together, and we basically smuggled goods. We used to get such goods and warehouses and re-sell it to make a penny or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned to us now that Brane was there, he was wearing a camouflage uniform. You also mentioned the police. Were there any other groups of men coming into the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, but Piko came in, as well as Rakic. Later, when I was released, those who managed to get out, like myself, talked among themselves, and I learned subsequently that it was Piko and Rakic who also came in from the so-called Red Berets. I don't know how it came about that Piko who was from Doboj, and Rakic to join the Red Berets in Teslic, I don't know under whose orders and who organised it all. The executive authorities should know better. Piko and Rakic could not have come from Doboj without someone from Teslic approving it first, and they were unfamiliar with me and my colleagues who were teachers, directors, or private entrepreneurs. So someone must have kept a list of people specifying who was engaged in what.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: During your detention at the TO warehouse, did you have to have any dealings with Piko or Rakic?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Not in the TO hangar. Later on, when I was taken for interrogation to the police station, it was Aleksa Petrovic who took me there, as well as Slobodan Radocic and Mirko Buba. They took me in a vehicle and to the police station for interrogation. Before that, I was taken to the hospital - or, rather, to an outpatient clinic that was there. It's not a hospital - because of my health. All of the doctors knew me from earlier. They knew my condition -- excuse me. I was received there. I was seated on a bench in -- in a -- in -- the duty office. There was a screen in the room. Some people from the TO came to the building. Raka and Piko were with them and another tall man. I never managed to find out who he is. I was told what his name was but I forgot. He was tall and dark-haired, but I didn't bother to memorize his name. They came in and asked whether Adil Isic -- sorry, Fadil Isic was there. He used to be the SDA president. Somebody said he was there behind the screen. Piko removed the screen and went in. I saw him pull out a handgun from his belt. He put the screen back, we heard a shot, and he left. The doctor came and said that I should go out through a side door. I was taken back to the TO, and then after an hour or two, they came for me again to take me to the station for interrogation. What I omitted to say was that Brane came in in the meantime and he beat Ramo, from Stenjaci. I can't recall his last name. He used to own horses. That's how he earned his livelihood. He was caught by someone up there in Stenjaci and taken to the TO. He came in and beat him heavily. When I was taken for interrogation, I saw a person tied to a tree in front of the station. 2 or 3 metres away there was a body covered in blood, and I recognised Ramo. Brane was there next to them. I don't know who the person who was tied to the tree was. He was -- Brane was still moving around, hitting him, after which I was taken inside. Aleksa Petrovic told me, You saw nothing, and I had to keep quiet. Although my conscience telling me it wasn't right not to tell anyone. In any case, I had to, to save my life.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: (redacted) redacted. Perhaps the witness should be reminded to avoid - unless it is wholly unavoidable for context - identifying himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the Judge's comment. Just make sure not to mention your first name or your last name. You can carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Very well. I'll do my best. All right, he said, it's up to you. If you don't give us 70.000 German marks, you won't be here by tonight. I just looked at him, wondering how can a man whom you know can look you in the eyes and tell you something like that, but I had to accept it. And it made me thinking, what to do. Then I asked Vlado for another cigarette, so, in five minutes, I think I had two or three cigarettes, because I was so nervous and so afraid. If I gave them money, they would kill me so that there would be no witnesses; if I didn't give them money they would kill me anyway. Therefore, I decided to give them the money, and I hoped that would extend my life for another two or three days, and that's why I agreed to give them the money. This is how the interrogation ended. I was sent back to the TO warehouse, but -- yes, I -- I came back on the same day. Aleksa Petrovic and Rakic came in a Golf car to pick me up. They took me out of the TO warehouse. Rakic said, you should go and take the money that you promised. I said, I don't have the key to my house or the key to my car. They're all at the police station. And he said, All right. He went to the police station, brought my car keys, but no other belongings such as my watch and things like that. He also brought the key to my house. When we reached my house, I asked him if I could take my crutches out of the car because I cannot climb up the stairs without them. He said it was okay. I entered the house, went to the upper floor. I had money in a number of bags. I counted the money. In the meantime, after I had promised the money and then went to the TO warehouse, a colleague of mine asked me, Ramo, do you have any money, and I said, Well, I used to have money in the house, unless it had been taken away. And he asked me, Would you give me some money to get out? And I said, If there's anything left, no problem. So I counted all the money, gave it to Rakic. I had some money left. Aleksa Petrovic was standing in front of my store, and I counted the money to Rakic inside the store, and they left. After half an hour, a colleague -- this colleague of mine came. He was brought by Rakic and he asked me, Do you have the money? And I gave him 5.000 German marks. He was immediately released, and this man paid this money back to me. He was the only one who paid the money back to me of all the others to whom I lent money, and he is currently living in the Netherlands and he was extremely grateful for the money that I gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sir, this person by the name of Rakic. You also earlier mentioned a person by the name of Raka. Are these one and the same person or are they two different persons?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Somebody called him Rakic; others used to call him Raka. When these berets came again to ask for money, I was looking for him, because I knew I gave the money to him, and he didn't give me any receipt whatsoever. I managed to find him, and I said, Rakic, people are coming asking for money but you took the money. I have no more money. And he started cursing and said, Tell them that you gave the money to Raka. So I heard it from him, calling himself Raka and cursing their mothers. He started writing a receipt and he took a piece of paper, just like I'm doing it now, and before he could finish it, he just decided to throw it away and told me, Just tell them that you gave the money to Raka. That was all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, after this event, did there come a time when you were released from the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I was released the following day. That day when I was interrogated and when I gave the money, it was the next day that I was released, but I was constantly under threat because they used to come repeatedly asking for money, but I finally solved this matter with Rakic. Then they took me to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Because Rako told me at the intersection in Teslic when I complained about not being able to sustain the pressure of asking for money, he used to tell me, You socialized too much with Pero Krgic [as interpreted] an inspector from Doboj this -- this Pejo Krnic investigated a fire that broke out in the youth centre and on that occasion, Pejo Krnic used to come to my place very often. That's when he told me, I'm not finished with you yet, because you were friends with Pejo Krnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If I could stop you there for a moment. Could you give us, if you know, the date of your release from the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. No, no, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you maybe tell us how long you were detained in the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: All in all, I spent 50 days in Tribinjes [as interpreted] and TO and in the jail and I know that very well, because I added all the days up. I don't know the dates though. I said that at one point I wanted to write my memoirs, something about the events that I experienced, but if I did that, it would have had to be very accurate because I would have had time to recall everything accurately. As it is, at this moment, I cannot remember any of those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, there's a term in the transcript that is not clear. You said you spent 50 days in the TO and in Tribinjes. That seems to be a wrong term. Can you clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you were detained there and for how long?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I was twice in Pribinic. First, I was taken by Raka, the second time I was taken by Dragan Babic; the latter asked for 6.000 German marks. I didn't have any money at that time. You used to go around to borrow some money and try to avoid being taken to Pribilic [as interpreted] but I did not have enough money that they asked for. So when we were detained in Pribilic [as interpreted] you couldn't distinguish between daylight and night-time. All the windows were boarded up and you could just try to keep track of time and date and the number of days that one spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But if you can give the Judges a rough indication perhaps of how many days were spent in the TO warehouse and how many days were spent in the Pribinic. Roughly. If you're able to give that figure.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I spent in Pribinic -- but the problem is I can't remember the dates but I think it was, all together, 12 or 15 days. We were taken from the Teslic jail to the TO, and the rest of the time I spent in the TO warehouse. And I spent two days from -- in the period between the 3rd of June and the 23rd of July I spent at home, because they let me go for those two days. So I was free for two days only. When they released me from the TO, I was taken to Pribinic, but I would have to calculate the individual portions of my detention. I just had a total figure in my head always.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. And what does the 23rd of July signify? What is that date?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, because this man Babic took me home and he told me to stay away out of their sight, that I would be killed otherwise, or detained again at Pribinic. So I used to hide in various villages up there, staying in the houses of my mother and other relatives. There were refugees from Darovar in my house, which was ordered by the civilian protection. Miro Cukovic was in charge of the civilian protection. He issued a paper which prevented me from collecting my prothesis and all the other aids that I needed, because I had no access to my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. When you say you didn't have access to your own home, what happened to -- to your home exactly?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: The house was confiscated and a certain Miso moved in from Darovar. I know that he was from Darovar. I didn't know that actually. When I came one day, I tried to unlock the door but it was impossible, and there was no tractor behind the house. I wondered what this was all about. I thought that someone had broken in. Then this man appeared and said, My name is Miso. I don't remember his last name; it was some 18 or 19 years ago. I asked him where he was from, and he said he was a refugee from Darovar and I asked him, How come that you are staying in my house? And he said that he had been given a paper by the civilian protection. He showed me the paper, which specified that I had no right to enter my house because everything had been confiscated. I wasn't even allowed to take my own personal belongings from the house. So what else could I do? I went back to my brother's house in Gornji Teslic. I tried, through the people I considered to be my friends, my Serb friends who turned out not to be my friends in fact, and I wanted to ask them to help me retrieve my house and move back again. They tried to go and see this Danilo Savic, the chief or the commander and there was another one called Kuzmanovic, I don't know which position they held of the two in order to have my house back, but they told me that for my own security it wouldn't be a good idea to go back to my home, that if I am fine living with my relatives, I should stay there. So it was a very difficult and very uncomfortable situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, are we still within the denied adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm just concluding that with my last question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, sir, after your release, did there come a time when you had to leave the municipality of Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, yes, I had to leave Teslic because I received a threatening letter, and this letter was handed over to the police station. There was a request in the letter for 35.000 German marks; otherwise, my house would be demolished. And I thought it was very risky, so I thought, if they're going to kill me in the place where I was born or in front of my mother's house, then I don't care. I got into my Skoda car and I drove through the so-called corridor and reached Raca. I was lucky, because they couldn't believe that a Muslim would dare drive a car along the Serbian corridor that was exclusively under their control and nobody else used it, so I really risked my life doing that and managed to reach Raca. And I entered Serbia and then I went to Croatia via Hungary. My wife and children were in Croatia because my brother had a flat in a place near Sibenik; the placed is called Pirovac. When I reached Pirovac, there was more activity than in Bosnia because the front line was some 8 kilometres away, and we managed to stay there until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And just to be clear, when exactly did you leave Teslic? Which month and year.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: On the 28th of December, in the morning, of 1992. There was some 10 centimetres of snow but I decided - it was a Monday, the 28th - that I would go no matter what, and I consciously took this risk and I'm still aware of this risk knowing that I could have been killed. So I ended up in hospital, this time because I took a risk again by coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. I know that a long time has elapsed since the events that we are discussing but I would appreciate your help in clarifying some of your evidence given today. You gave your first statement to the OTP investigators in August of 2000; and then in July of 2003, you met them again, and, on that occasion, you wanted to make some corrections in your original statement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that even today. I can make some corrections because it depends on one's memory. As I said, if you want to be accurate and write a book about it, then you should do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. In your statements, as well as today, you described these men who used to come there while you were detained, and you said that -- you called Brane Milicic and the men who surrounded him, Sarenjaci. Then you mentioned the Red Berets, Piko and Rakic, i.e., Raka. Did these two groups have identical uniforms? Did they all wear camouflage uniforms and red berets?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the difference was.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Piko and Raka wore olive-drab uniforms; whereas, the others had camouflage army uniforms, similar to the ones worn nowadays by the US troops. That's what Brane used to wear, and that's why we called them Sarenjaci. We were terrified whenever they would burst into the warehouse, TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any other paramilitary formations there in Teslic, apart from the ones that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, Piko, that was Red Berets. They were the people who did not come from the Teslic territory. Piko and Raka and their organisation. They were from outside, not from Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You saw no Arkan's units at that time in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't see any of them, and I don't know about them. I didn't see any Arkan insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dragan Babic and the guards in Pribinic. Can you tell us what uniforms and what insignia they had?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: How should I tell you? Dragan Babic used to have five or six of his men and they would go around the village, around the villages and arrest people. If they knew that there was a person with some money, they would take that person to Pribinic, they would beat them up, break bones and force them in various means. He also used to wear a military uniform -- excuse me. And his people took from Saban Mesinovic a car, Ascona [Realtime transcript read in error "Skoda"]. Saban Mesinovic used to be a taxi driver. He used to have an Ascona, which for us at the time was a very good car. So they took the car and they would use it. Not Skoda, Ascona. You have to correct this thing here. It is not Skoda. All right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In relation to your arrest and that taking of money from you, in November 1992, you were interviewed by an investigative judge from the basic court in Teslic as a victim of a crime.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I don't know his name. Aha, Nenad Kovacevic. Yes, it was him. So I think there was some sort of a hearing and not only me but many other people as well were interviewed. People who had to hand over their money and other things. People who were forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And at that occasion, you stated -- you basically repeated part of what you said today and you said that you gave the money to Raka. However, you also said that you gave 1400 billion at the time or 140.000 dinars at the time of the giving of the statement. Was there some sort of a change in the money system meanwhile? (redacted)s

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: (redacted) I myself also wouldn't say it if I were you. I would also be afraid to say it. This Nenad is still alive and is very familiar with the case. He handled the case in a very correct way and currently he is a practicing lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we should redact the transcript. Page 45, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, you probably did not see the decision to open investigation and detain Raka and others. You are, however, aware that they had been detained because they took part in that proceedings in which you testified.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I knew very well that they were "detained," in inverted commas, I have to say. You know, that was the sort of practice they had there at the time. Because if you detain someone whom you had organised in the first place to go there and do these things, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now when Piko, Raka and other members of the Red Berets were arrested, do you know that there -- at the time two people were killed during the arrest?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Two people were killed? I don't know. Maybe I heard it and now I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that judge told you that. But you didn't see the original request to start the investigation by the competent prosecutor and the decision to start the investigation. We have here both documents, and both documents contain the names of those person who committed numerous crimes. And, among other names, your name is mentioned as well. However, as opposed to other people who were also forced to hand over cars, money and valuables, you can find the following amounts. Mujo Sahic?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: No, no. Not Sabic, Sahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mujo Sahic, 2.000 German marks; Slavko Vidic, 7.000 German marks; Jozo Martinovic, 34.500 German marks, 3.000 Swiss francs, 23.000 Austrian schillings. And, at the end, there's your name as well, I'm not going to mention it. And the amount is 140.000 dinars. So these people while they were interrogated, they gave the correct amounts and those amounts were entered into the record. Both in the original request and the subsequent decision to start the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you? Why did they break Martinovic's hand later on? You know, he used to be a carpenter. And then Mujo Sahic, how much did he give? I know him. I used to be there with him and this other guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, I'm sorry. I'm simply telling you that other names have certain other amounts and not only dinars but also foreign currency, while you said to that judge only that you gave this amount in dinars without any further explanation. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Can I ask you something, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Here I am asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: But I want to ask you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, that's not allowed.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the transcript here says - I don't know if this is an error in the transcript - that Mr. Aleksic said, "You said to the judge what you gave..." But we don't know what the witness said at the time. What we have is the document only. So not to mislead the witness as to what is said and what was written. What you have a document and what's written on it is all we can say. And perhaps it would be easier to show it to the witness, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's P1363. And in B/C/S, it's the last page. In English, it's page 160 and 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which tab is this in your list, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's your tab number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see, it says here at the bottom of the page: "When we reached my house, I told Raka that, as I did not supply the goods myself, I would raise the amount to 140.000 billion. So I gave him the money. Nowadays the amount is 140.000 dinars. Raka left me at home and my detention was over on that day. That was on the 12th of June, 1992." Do you see that that is what you stated at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: You mean before that court? Before Nenad Kovacevic? Well, I know Nenad. We know each other very well. He was rather careless when he drafted this text and it was his decision. That's what he said, in order for me not to have any other problems. You know, when I was sitting in his office he even brought out some rakija for the two of us to drink, if you really want to know all the details about the case. So I also sued that Miso for my house, I wanted him to return my house. And Nenad told me, Let it lie. Other better times will come. So Nenad and I agreed on some sort of friendly solution. It wasn't a actual act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you state that you were released on the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: No, it was the 12th of July. That's when I gave the money, that's when they took two vans full of goods from my store. I didn't see that, but my aunt and my uncle saw it. And also another relative; he was deaf and dumb. And they were watching all this happening from their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. But today you stated that you were released the day after.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes, I was released the day after. I wasn't released on the same day. On that day I gave the money. I told you that this is some sort of a friendly indictment, so that they could show that they did something in relation to those people and those events. That's how it was. I really want to explain you what exactly happened there. And this Nenad maybe even saved me. He told me, I am going to pronounce a positive judgement if you want to sue for the return of your house, but somebody is going to kill you later on. You have to be careful with those Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you stated that you were released on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Yes, on the 13th. On the 12th I gave the money, on the 12th, they took the goods, and then the day after they released me. Raka came, took me out, and brought me to the house the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So if you were arrested on the 3rd and released on the 13th, it means that, in that first period, you spent ten days there. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, the witness said the 12th of July, not June. He just said July. Page 49, line 4: "No, it was the 12th of July."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, page 49, I asked was it on the 12th of June? And then he said, No, it wasn't on the 12th of July but the day after. And in the statement you can find it was the 12th of June. That's what the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you're reading. But I see here, "Did you state that you were released on the 12th of June?" And he replied, "No, it was the 12th of July."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June. June. Not July, now I -- now I see. I didn't have my spectacles on. It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, at the end of this statement, you say: "This is all I have to say. There is no need for read out aloud the text to me because I listened while it was dictated and I can state that it is correct." And the date here is the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you had no comments, no comments to what the investigative judge wrote at the time.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I told you, it was a friendly agreement. The purpose was to show that something was being done about the Red Berets, you know, as if they had been arrested and as if a real indictment had been brought forward. You can accept that. You don't have to. But I can guarantee that that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Aleksic. We will return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, it has been brought to our attention by the interpreters that the exchange between yourself and the witness shortly before the break, as regards the date, the answer that the witness gave, that it is unclear as to whether the witness, at the end -- at the end of it said June or July, so it would assist if you could return to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have your statement before you, you provided to the investigating judge on the 19th of November. Before the break, I read to you that you purportedly said that that was all had you to say and no records had to be read back to you, because you were following the process of typing it in and that it is correct. Then, in 1992, you stated that you were released on the 12th of June of that year. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: I do. However, what were the circumstances under which I managed to achieve that? That's what remains to be said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: What were the circumstances under which I had to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before the break, you said that it was a friendly conversation because you shared a glass of brandy with the judge.

utterances.speaker: ST-008
utterances.text: Well, I explained the conditions to you, and if you failed to understand it, then who will?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
